debate_title: Should frontier AI developers be legally liable for harms...

conflicts.point: Whether upstream foundation model developers or downstream deployers bear primary causal responsibility for mitigating runtime harms.

positions.stance: Upstream developers must bear legal liability because they control training data and architectural guardrails that downstream users cannot inspect or modify.
Liability must attach at the execution boundary where commercial deployers handle user interfaces and maintain runtime logs.

conflicts.point: Whether pre-deployment safety audits and compute floors protect the public or serve as regulatory moats for dominant technology firms.

positions.stance: Mandatory audits are a necessary institutional safeguard against unrecoverable systemic risks from powerful AI systems.
Audit mandates and infrastructure thresholds function primarily as corporate indemnity shields that protect dominant firms while blocking legal redress for injured consumers.

verdicts.conflict: Whether upstream foundation model developers or downstream deployers bear primary causal responsibility for mitigating runtime harms.
verdicts.rationale: Both positions capture valid parts of the causal chain. Safetyists correctly note that upstream developers control training data and base architectures, while accelerationists correctly identify that runtime harms occur at the deployment interface where users interact with the system.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Long-term liability litigation results showing whether courts assign fault primarily to base model design flaws or specific deployment contexts.
